courseReview.method: Read every complete actual enriched profile, formal prerequisite and offering, with legacy descriptions available alongside. Profile-derived content has particular weight. All 42 original courses were inspected; two weak choices removed, leaving 40 active unique courses and 72 placements.

courses.name: Personal & Professional Development
courses.profile: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate student formation, namely, actively, consciously and ethically relating to oneself, others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhances critical thinking and independent learning. It also helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners. The course stimulates core academic skills, namely: Select and critically analyze academic sources Articulate research questions, thesis statements and arguments Improve communication skills through various forms of writing and speaking activities The course fosters personal, social and civic competencies, namely: Craft own academic and personal learning goals Critically reflect on own learning Develop effective collaborative learning approaches with peers, instructors and external partners Valuing community engagement, including the value of different knowledge types and perspectives
courses.legacyDescription: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
courses.contribution: develops critical source use, academic communication, ethical reflection and professional engagement

courses.name: Introduction to Economics
courses.profile: This course provides an introduction to the principles of economics. The first part of the course delves into microeconomics concepts, including supply and demand, game theory, theory of consumer behaviour, theory of the firm and market structure. The seco nd part of the course covers macroeconomics, beginning with an exploration of macroeconomics events and fundamental concepts such as aggregate output, unemployment and inflation rate. It then examines the dynamics of goods and financial markets in the short run.
courses.legacyDescription: Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.
courses.contribution: Specific complementary microeconomic and macroeconomic concepts clarify markets, firms and aggregate change; not a dedicated history of capitalism or emerging economies.

courses.name: International Macroeconomics
courses.profile: This course explores the economy as a whole by examining its dynamics over the short, medium, and long run. Key indicators such as national income, economic growth, inflation, and unemployment are studied. The course analyses how fiscal and monetary polici es affect the economy. It also covers business cycles, economic crises, and international trade, providing the tools needed to interpret economic data, evaluate policy decisions, and understand global economic trends.
courses.legacyDescription: Study the economy as a whole through topics such as national income, economic growth, inflation, and unemployment. Understand how governments and central banks use fiscal and monetary policies to influence economic performance over time. The course also explores business cycles, international trade, and economic crises, preparing students to evaluate policy debates and global economic trends.
courses.contribution: Specific complementary growth, business-cycle, policy and international-trade theory supports interpretation of economic change; it does not supply historical case research.

courses.name: Microeconomics & Behavior
courses.profile: This course provides a comprehensive exploration of advanced topics in microeconomic theory. Structured in three parts, the course begins with an in-depth analysis of consumer behaviour, including decision-making under uncertainty, non -egoistic preferences, and cognitive limitations. The second part analyses market structures with an emphasis on imperfect competition, strategic behaviour, and the functioning of factor markets. The final part of the course covers general equilibrium and market efficiency, investigating externalities and the role of government in the economy. Throughout the course, students will engage with research papers through presentations and discussions, bridging theoretical concepts with empirical evidence.
courses.legacyDescription: Study how consumers and producers make decisions under scarcity. Explore key concepts such as rational choice, decision-making under uncertainty, and non-egoistic preferences. Analyze market structures, strategic interactions, and factor markets. Learn how markets function and examine the impact of regulation. Develop analytical tools to better understand behavior and engage with empirical research.
courses.contribution: Specific complementary consumer behaviour, market structures, strategic interaction and efficiency support analysis of economic institutions, without claiming historical instruction.

courses.name: Public Economics
courses.profile: This course examines the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy affects efficiency and equity. It explores the rationale for government intervention and key concepts such as market failure, public goods, externalities, taxation, p ublic spending, redistribution, and political economy. By combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, the course provides a framework for analysing the economic impact of public policies.
courses.legacyDescription: Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.
courses.contribution: Specific complementary taxation, spending, redistribution and political economy provide analytical tools for studying inequality; not a dedicated historical sequence.

courses.name: Econometrics
courses.profile: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.
courses.legacyDescription: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.
courses.contribution: Direct quantitative method contribution: OLS, GLS, instrumental variables, tests and an empirical paper; applying these to historical evidence is a possible use, not a required historical assignment.

courses.name: Behavioral Economics
courses.profile: This course integrates insights from psychology into economic theory to better understand how people make decisions. Learn how actual behavior deviates from the predictions of traditional economic models due to biases, heuristics, and framing. Through experiments, students will deepen their understanding of decision-making and its implications for economic theory and practice.
courses.legacyDescription: This course integrates insights from psychology into economic theory to better understand how people make decisions. Learn how actual behavior deviates from the predictions of traditional economic models due to biases, heuristics, and framing. Through experiments, students will deepen their understanding of decision-making and its implications for economic theory and practice.
courses.contribution: Removed: organisational psychology/behavioural decision theory does not make a sufficiently specific historical contribution to this option. Replaced with actual art history and historiography already in the verified palette.

courses.name: Research Methods & Statistics
courses.profile: Research Methods & Statistics is a general introduction in research methodology and statistics. The introduction to methodology includes the logics and design of research (e.g., operationalization, experimental design, sampling), and some specific techniques (e.g., laboratory research, surveys). The introduction to statistics includes descriptive and inferential statistics, covering measures of central tendency, spread, association, univariate and bivariate inferential statistics, and analysis of variance. This course includes an introduction to simple applications of multivariate statistics but most coverage of multivariate statistics and statistical modelling will be covered in the course HCBPSYC211 Statistics & Experimental Methods in Health & Behavioral Sciences. The first 9 course weeks (not including the semester break) of the course provide the theoretical background. This includes not only instruction and practice in basic research methodology and statistics, but also the planning stages of the group research projects that will dominate the latter portion of the semester. In this portion of the semester, students of each section attend two classes each week with their instructor. Project groups are formed, and these groups work together in applying newly learned concepts to their own research problem thru individually completed homework exercises, and through sharing and discussing their progress with the rest of the class. The final 6 course weeks are dedicated exclusively to group project work. This research project can fall within any academic discipline.
courses.legacyDescription: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.
courses.contribution: teaches research design, operationalisation, sampling and descriptive and inferential statistics

courses.name: Psychology of Organizations & Leadership
courses.profile: People are the organisation. Without people, organisations cannot survive or be productive. This course, tailored for Liberal Arts and Sciences bachelor students, offers an interdisciplinary exploration of the psychological, social, and structural dynamics within organisations. It equips students with the knowledge and skills needed to navigate and influence organisational environments effectively throughout their academic and professional careers. Drawing on foundational and contemporary research in organisational behaviour, this upper- level undergraduate course incorporates a case-based approach that includes conceptual frameworks, case discussions, and skill-building activities. Students will explore topics such as motivation, leadership, group dynamics, and organizational culture using Robbins and Judge’s (2023) Organisational Behaviour as a primary resource. Additional literature and materials will supplement the course to provide a well-rounded perspective. Topics Covered => Core Concepts: Diversity in organisations, attitudes and job satisfaction, emotions and moods, personality and values, perception and decision-making, motivation, communication, leadership, power and politics, and conflict and negotiation. Structural Dynamics: The structure and culture of organisations, group behaviour, work teams, and organisational change. These topics are structured within a comprehensive model that defines the field of organisational behaviour and outlines its key concepts and relationships.
courses.legacyDescription: This course offers Liberal Arts and Sciences students a deep dive into the psychological, social, and structural dynamics that shape workplaces. Through interactive case discussions, simulations, and real-world insights, students develop critical skills in motivation, leadership, group dynamics, and culture. By synthesizing research and applying theory to practice, participants gain the tools to navigate and influence diverse organizational environments effectively.
courses.contribution: Removed: organisational psychology/behavioural decision theory does not make a sufficiently specific historical contribution to this option. Replaced with actual art history and historiography already in the verified palette.

courses.name: Law, Society & Justice
courses.profile: This course offers three different perspectives on the law: the legal, the social and the normative. We spend the first part of the course exploring the definitions of law and the different understandings of law in a general sense. We take a brief look at the different legal systems of the world, and we discuss various fields of law: constitutional law, administrative law, criminal law, international law and human rights, as well as select fields of private law including property law, contract and torts law. After the Fall break, students consider the relationships between law and society and the concept of justice. In addition to reading and discussing the main principles within each field of law, we explore these through reading case law and performing trial simulations.
courses.legacyDescription: Examines law from legal, socio‑scientific and normative perspectives. Explores definitions, legal traditions and fields of law, investigates the relationship between law and society and the concept of justice, and includes case law, excursion to international legal organisations, interviews with practitioners and a moot court session.
courses.contribution: Specific complementary legal, social and normative approaches to institutions and justice support inquiry into state authority; this is not a historical-methods course.

courses.name: Modern History
courses.profile: This course gives a chronological overview of history in the modern period (1815-2025). The nineteenth century saw the rise of industrial societies and of the new political ideals of popular sovereignty (e.g. Marxism, socialism) and national self-determination. These forces continued to operate in the twentieth century, which was characterized by tremendous upheavals like the Russian Revolution, the two World Wars and the demise of communism in Eastern Europe. The course offers a survey of the main economic, political and cultural developments from 1815 to the present. Special attention will be paid to the relationship between economic developments and the international changes of the Balance of Power. A number of issues of seminal importance to modern history will be analysed thoroughly: the revolutions of the 19th century, the Belle Epoque, the origins of the First World War, the Great Depression, and the Second World War, the Cold War and the rise of the welfare state, the decolonization process, and the European economic and monetary co-operation between nations.
courses.legacyDescription: Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.
courses.contribution: provides a chronological survey of modern political, economic and cultural history from 1815

courses.name: Histories of Gender
courses.profile: This course explores the histories and lives of children and young and older adults, through the lens of gender within an American context. The education takes place in a safe environment where critical thought thrives. The time frame is the 19th through the 21st centuries. Thematic topics unfold within a chronological framework. They include slavery in the nineteenth century, surviving and thriving in the twentieth century, and individual and community activism today. The approach centers storytelling. Throughout the term we explore the significance of the ways gendered stories are told by i.e., educational institutions, in children’s storybooks, within the medical community, across social media, through cultural expressions and forms, and by individual people. For instance, class members conduct interviews of elderly Queer folks and interpret their findings by drawing from scholars including bell hooks and Kimberle Crenshaw. They also contribute to the semester long Walking with Pride Project, an activist artwork woven by students, Queer and multiply marginalized people world-wide, and their allies. The rug features digitally in https://thewalkingwithprideproject.wordpress.com/, and physically in cultural spaces internationally. Finally, students explore repression, resistance, and/or retribution in their final project, where they choose both the content of their research, ranging from transphobia to banned books, as well as the form, including but not limited to, an essay, podcast, graphic novel, or artistic expression.
courses.legacyDescription: Explores lives of ordinary people through the lens of gender from the 19th to 21st centuries. Uses storytelling across cultural forms; topics include slavery, mid‑20th‑century life, conversion therapy, queer cinema and banned books; engages with projects like Walking With Pride.
courses.contribution: Direct social/cultural history through gender, storytelling and marginalised lives in the nineteenth- to twenty-first-century United States, including interviews and interpretive projects.

courses.name: History of Empires
courses.profile: This course is about great powers, superpowers and even hyperpowers. ‘Empire’ is a powerful and dangerous word. It has a rich and ambiguous history and strong polemical connotations now and in the past. The typical empire is usually presented as oppressive and ruthless, although some of the modern empires are democracies that focus upon the improvements of its society. This course deals with some of the most important empires in World History. Next to this some of the most important theories on empires will be treated. How is the rise and fall of empires explained? What are the sources of empire and how are great power politics conducted?
courses.legacyDescription: Examines the rise and fall of empires and the contested concept of empire. Discusses oppressive and benevolent features of empires, covers key theories on empires and power politics and analyses major historical examples.
courses.contribution: compares empires, imperial power and theories of their rise, rule and decline across world history

courses.name: Western Way of War
courses.profile: This course gives a chronological overview of the history of Warfare in the Western World from antiquity to the present day. All aspects of war on land, sea, and in the air are covered: weapons and technology; strategy and tactics; discipline and intelligence; mercenaries and standing armies; cavalry and infantry; chivalry and Blitzkrieg; guerrilla assault and nuclear arsenals. The central controversial thesis of this course is that war in western societies has followed a unique path leading to the Western hegemony of the world. From Greek hoplites, Roman legionnaires to the jet plane and cruise missile, war has served as the driving force behind the West’s rise to global domination. The history of the West, both at home and overseas, has centred around ferocious competition for mastery among uncompromisingly ambitious powers, in which the ruthless, innovative, and the decisive displaced the complacent, the imitative, and the irresolute.
courses.legacyDescription: Provides a chronological overview of warfare in the Western world from antiquity to the present. Covers weapons, technology, strategy, defence, mercenaries, cavalry, chivalry, Blitzkrieg, guerrilla warfare and nuclear arsenals, illustrating competition for mastery in Western history.
courses.contribution: traces warfare, technology, state power and conflict from antiquity to the present

courses.name: Native American Histories
courses.profile: This Social and Cultural History course (the study of people and their expressions) introduces Native American histories and life from the 19th through the 21st century. Throughout the term we work with Indigenous students, professors, experts, and elders to explore topics including the “Stolen Lives” of Indian children forcibly taken from their homes and placed in Indian Boarding Schools from the 1830’s through the 1990’s, human trafficking, Traditional Ecological Knowledge (TEK) and cultural resistance and regeneration that play out in language revival, food ways, and Indigenous music, art, and film. Our readings, activities and conversations draw from Indigenous methodologies that center storytelling, respect, and reciprocity. We also draw from Indigenous understanding of knowledge as relational, embodied and practiced rather than abstract, extractive, and memorized. An example is the activist artwork at the center of our first collaboration. It is crafted collectively, mobile, and sustained through relationships over time, rather than something that is created by one person into a finished product that is owned by another person. The fields of gender studies, psychology and sociology help us understand the presence of the past in Native American history and life, especially when we explore childhood, migration, trauma, and family matters.
courses.legacyDescription: This course introduces students to Native American history and life from the 19th through the 21st century.  It argues that power, fear, misogyny, education, genocide, and resilience shape the Indigenous past and present. Topics we explore include the “Stolen Lives” of Indian children forcibly taken from their homes and placed in Indian Boarding Schools from the 1830’s through the 1990’s; Murdered and Missing Indigenous Women and Girls in the twenty-first century; and the individual and community forms of cultural resistance and environmental regeneration that connect past with present and future generations. We learn from the Native American scholars and 2Spirit youth that speak to and with the class. Exchange of cultural and intellectual knowledge also happens when we work with Lakota students to address contemporary challenges. Legislation, memoir, novels, and Indigenous children’s stories are central to our studies. So are the analyses of contemporary music and artistic expressions and exhibitions, as well as Hollywood and Indigenous film featuring Native American histories and lives.
courses.contribution: studies Indigenous histories, forced assimilation, resistance, memory and cultural regeneration

courses.name: History Research Seminar
courses.profile: In the summer of 1809 the British sailed some 40,000 soldiers and 5,000 horses in 500 navy vessels over the English Channel to land in Walcheren. This greatest amphibious operation in Napoleonic times became know as the Walcheren Expedition or the Expedition to the Scheldt. The ultimate British goal was to occupy the important harbour of Antwerp. On the other side, Dutch and French forces, including many foreign troops like Irish, German and Polish were trying to stop the British assault. The outcome of the Walcheren Expedition not only left a big mark on local history, but also had an enormous impact on the Netherlands, France, Great Brittain and international politics in general. In this course we will research the primary sources about the Walcheren expedition. Think about diaries, letters, memoirs and official reports written by soldiers, officers or officials form all participants in this conflict. You will learn how to search for, read and analyse these primary sources, through writing a course-filling paper; as such, this course will require a lot of self-study and fewer class meetings.
courses.legacyDescription: Guides students through the full arc of historical inquiry, from formulating research questions to engaging critically with sources. Emphasises methodological rigour and interdisciplinary thinking and culminates in a substantial research paper.
courses.contribution: Direct primary-source inquiry on the 1809 Walcheren Expedition through diaries, letters, memoirs and reports, culminating in a substantial paper. Not an unrestricted Economic History thesis.

courses.name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
courses.profile: This course offers a broad approach to human rights: the legal, the historical and the theoretical/philosophical. In the first part of the course, human rights will mainly be studied in a legal way, adopting a legal perspective. Students will be introduced to the catalogue of human rights as positive law. Human rights treaties, the monitoring mechanisms and case law on human rights will be explored. This knowledge will be tested in a mid-term exam (multiple choice). In the second part, students will delve into a more historical and philosophical understanding of human rights. We will investigate the rise of the language of human rights in the 17th and 18th century, its culmination in the US Bill of Rights (1791) and the Déclaration des Droits de l’Homme et du Citoyen (1789). We will explore the further developments of the language in the 20th century in particular, which brought a great extension of the number and application of human rights. Students will read landmark cases that touch upon contentious, and often politicised disputes between liberty and equality. Some emphasis in this course will be given to natural law and its connection to human rights. We will delve into the classical and medieval scholarship on natural law, starting with Plato’s and Aquinas’ views on right and wrong. This will be compared to the modern views on the same going back to Hobbes and Locke, the latter considered to be the founding father of the rights paradigm. Human rights in today’s traditional societies will be investigated through selected case studies.
courses.legacyDescription: Offers a legal, historical and philosophical approach to human rights. Studies classical and modern philosophers, traces the rise of human rights, examines the US Bill of Rights and the French Declaration, and discusses human rights treaties.
courses.contribution: traces human rights through positive law, historical development and philosophical argument

courses.name: Introduction to Public International Law
courses.profile: This course serves as a general introduction to public international law as a field of study and professional discipline. Designed to provide you with a foundational knowledge of the creation and the historical evolution of the subject, it is broadly divided into three parts. The first part deals with general principles of international law such as its sources, subjects, and organization. In the second part, the focus shifts to specific domains, namely the regulation of the use of force, the law of armed co nflict, international criminal law, refugee law, and environmental law. The final part addresses the politics of international law as it delves into issues such as the right to self-determination, Third World Approaches to International Law, and questions of treaty negotiation, compliance and effectiveness. The general purpose of the course is to shed light on some of the most important questions of international law both from a formal legal and a social science perspective. Performance in the course will be assessed through in-class exercises, a preparatory and an open book exam, a podcast and a reflection report.
courses.legacyDescription: Introduces rules, institutions and politics of public international law. Covers treaties, the UN, armed conflict, war crimes, refugee protection and climate change. Students analyse cases, debate issues and produce a podcast connecting law to global challenges.
courses.contribution: examines the historical evolution, institutions and doctrines of international law and armed conflict

courses.name: Comparative Constitutional Law
courses.profile: In this course on constitutional law and administrative law, students will undertake an exploration of the essential principles of these foundational legal fields. A comparative approach is used, examining and analyzing the constitutional law of five different legal systems. A constitution is the “fundamental and organic law of a nation or state that establishes the institutions and apparatus of government, defines the scope of governmental sovereign powers, and guarantees individual civil rights and civil liberties”, and ther efore, constitutional law is the “field of law dealing with aspects of constitutional provisions, such as restrictions on government powers and guarantees of rights.” (Blacks Law Dictionary 8 Ed, Garner et al eds, West 2004.) Yet, constitutional law is so much more than is suggested by these definitions. At the center of the modern constitutional state is the law, which protects peace, freedom and security. It is this law that is controlling, not the human actors in a state. In order that all may have acce ss to and rely on it, this law should be enshrined in a written document. Democracy demands a law that is enacted by a legislative body after public debate about its contents. The foundational values of a legal culture are written down in its constitution. The constitution takes up established values, tried and tested institutions and reliable political experience and passes them on to the next generation in a binding manner.
courses.legacyDescription: Explores constitutional law and state organisation, using a comparative approach. Covers constitutionalism, separation of powers, judicial review, federalism and fundamental rights, and discusses constitution‑making, religious constitutions and constitutional backsliding.
courses.contribution: compares constitutional institutions, state power, rights and administrative authority

courses.name: Foundations of European Union Law
courses.profile: EU law is everywhere, from the very strict new rules on data-protection that literally pop-up with every website you open, to less apparent instances such as the EU rules on reducing plastic bags that have found their way into distinct and different national laws throughout the EU. European law by now significantly affects the legal order in European countries and reflects as well as shapes the process of European integration in multiple ways. This course introduces you to the EU legal order by familiarizing you first with the institutional framework of the European Union and the organization of its legal foundations in particular. We will then survey the key substantive areas of EU law that revolve around EU fundamental rights, citizenship, and the freedom of movement of persons, workers, goods and establishments. You will be equipped to understand the EU legal order and research its manifestations both at the EU level as well as in the domestic context in which most of the EU law manifests itself in the lives of citizens, consumers, businesses and governments. There will also be guest lectures to further illustrate EU law and its functioning in theory and practice. The course is divided in two main parts. In the first part we will jointly examine the procedural aspects of EU law through a combination of brief lectures, in-class exercises and discussions. In the second part we will study the substantive law of the EU through the method of Problem Based Learning. Students will study a relevant case using the seven-step PBL method.
courses.legacyDescription: Introduces the EU legal order. Studies institutions, framework, citizenship and the internal market using problem‑based exercises and guest lectures.
courses.contribution: examines European integration, EU institutions and the interaction of European and national legal orders

courses.name: Introduction to Political Philosophy
courses.profile: In the course Introduction to Political Philosophy we shall examine the views on the nature of man, of society, and of political authority held by a number of influential Western thinkers. By the means of their particular political theories, the thinkers in question certainly intended to contribute to the solution of problems affecting the communities they were part of and their time. We shall look at the intellectual presuppositions of their theories and compare the problems they intended to solve, as well as their solutions, with the most significant actual political problems, the perception the general public opinion has of them and our current solutions. In particular, we shall focus on the authors’ justification for the existence and organization of political power. The course aims to provide a comprehensive introduction to the nature, characters, and purposes of each of the various political theories examined, from classical antiquity to today. To achieve this goal it is designed as informative and critical. Students are expected to master a number of relevant items and to assess form and quality of the influence that certain political theories have had, and may still have, on present day politics. In the attempt to determine whether there are ‘perennial’ political problems and features, students are expected to constantly compare past and present, and to find out what are the possible connections between empirical and normative political science.
courses.legacyDescription: Introduces political philosophy. Examines concepts such as authority, freedom, equality, democracy, human rights, pluralism, multiculturalism, poverty and environmental issues through classical and contemporary texts. Emphasises essay writing and presentations.
courses.contribution: places influential theories of society, authority and justice in their historical settings

courses.name: Foundations of Comparative Politics
courses.profile: All over the world people seem increasingly dissatisfied with the way their political system works, whether its citizens in Bangladesh who ousted the Hasina government, or voters in consolidated democracies like Sweden who are increasingly voting for parties at the left and right extremes of the political spectrum. How can we understand and explain these developments? Foundations of comparative politics provides you with the key analytical tools to analyze and compare political systems and the development and functioning of democracies in particular. This is done using the research tools of ‘mainstream’ political science: theory driven qualitative and quantitative empirical research that seeks to describe and/or explain political phenomena. The course provides an overview and analysis of the core structures and institutions of political systems by examining the position of the state and studying its internal structures and functioning and its interaction with society. We examine these issues using the conceptual toolbox of comparative politics. We familiarize ourselves with the basic institutions that make up political institutions, and the way democracies and authoritarian regimes develop and can break down. We examine the functioning of consolidated democracies and the challenges they face from developments such as the decline of political parties, mediatization, the rising importance of non- majoritarian institutions such as courts and impact of globalization and internationalization on the capacity of domestic governments to act.
courses.legacyDescription: Provides analytical tools to compare political systems and democracies. Examines phenomena like democratic backsliding, decline of political parties, rise of populism, media changes, non‑majoritarian institutions and globalization’s impact on domestic politics.
courses.contribution: compares political systems, democratisation, institutions, parties and contemporary political change

courses.name: Theory of International Relations
courses.profile: Brewing wars in the South China Sea, the Middle East, and Europe, trade wars, global climate change, amongst a plethora of other crises and difficulties, show the importance of understanding International Relations and geopolitics. This course gives the student a basic understanding of International Relations through a historical and contemporary scope. You work with a textbook to understand the different schools of thought within International Relations and then use historical or contemporary topics to apply these theories to. This will be achieved by group presentations. Your knowledge will be further increased by homework assignments and an exam. Finally, you end the course with a United Nations Security Council Simulation, where you take on the role of one of the UNSC members, and plead your country’s case in a current problem of international relations.
courses.legacyDescription: Introduces basic theories of international relations and applies them to contemporary issues such as climate change, energy, humanitarian intervention, global crises and international relations between North-South and South-South actors. Includes a UN Security Council negotiation simulation.
courses.contribution: uses historical and contemporary cases to test theories of international relations and geopolitics

courses.name: European Union Politics
courses.profile: This course introduces you to the European Union, a body politic that has been characterized as diverse as Unidentified Political Object, an unimperial empire as well as a superstate. Whatever its nickname , the EU is as political as any other body invested with public authority. For political scientists this means that it is vital to understand its functioning and to see where power is exercised and how various state and non-state interests try to get their preferences turned into policies. In the first part of the course we outline key actors, institutions and decision -making rules and show how political scientists have employed various ways to study EU politics and policy- making. Students will engage in Navigating the EU exercises that show them EU politics in the making and the sources to be used for that. In the second part of the course we will more directly examine the clash of interests through a group based research project where you study a legislative dossier and the interaction between interest groups and Members of the European Parliament, using the E Us transparency register . A key focal point in this analysis concerns the relative power of business interests vis a vis other interests in EU - decisionmaking and assessing what this implies for the legitimacy and effectiveness of EU - policies.
courses.legacyDescription: Introduces EU politics. Outlines actors, institutions and decision‑making rules; examines responses to crises; and employs various approaches to study EU politics and policy‑making.
courses.contribution: analyses EU institutions, decision-making, public authority and competing state and non-state interests

courses.name: Peace & Conflict
courses.profile: Peace and Conflict Studies is an interdisciplinary field that explores the causes, consequences, and potential solutions to both violent and nonviolent conflicts. Its goal is to understand the complex factors that contribute to conflict, the dynamics of violence, and the strategies for achieving lasting peace. The field encompasses insights from history, sociology, political science, international relations, and law, among other disciplines . This course introduces the field by examining and assessing multi ple theories of conflict and peacebuilding in the context of ongoing and past conflicts at regional, national and international levels. Peace and Conflict Studies is not only interdisciplinary but also shaped by diverse analytical perspectives. Some approaches emphasize structural inequality , clashing ideologies, and others focus on humiliation, historical wounds, and identity -based grievances, particularly in colonial or postcolonial contexts. Each lens draws attention to different forms of evidence and different peacebuilding strategies. As a result, this course demonstrates the importance of adopting a holistic approach that includes in ternational, institutional, and state -led elements, as well as cultural, interpersonal, and bottom-up actions led by civil society. The course uses “Travelling Concepts” as a tool for critically applying an interdisciplinary perspective. Students will compare how “justice,” “truth,” or “reconciliation” are mobilized in legal vs.
courses.legacyDescription: Introduces Peace & Conflict Studies. Examines definitions of peace and conflict; analyzes conflict causation, violence typologies and radicalisation; applies reconciliation and conflict‑transformation models to real‑world scenarios through lectures and portfolio work.
courses.contribution: integrates history, sociology, politics and law in the study of conflict, violence and peacebuilding

courses.name: Introduction to Sociology
courses.profile: Sociology provides a diverse and intricate toolkit composed of concepts, methods, and theories, which aids in comprehending and dissecting the functioning of societies on a local scale and the complex interconnections triggering global phenomena. Unlike disciplines like economics or political science, the subject of sociological inquiry is less clearly de fined. It encompasses all facets of human engagement within society, spanning from everyday interactions to the most longstanding social institutions. As a result, the wealth of knowledge within sociology can feel daunting, leaving one uncertain about where to begin. The course follows the recommendations 3 of the Sociological Literacy Framework 1, which is composed of the essential concepts and competencies in the discipline, as portrayed in the following table: Furthermore, this course overviews some of the most impactful sociological theories, including those by Marx, Weber, Durkheim, and Du Bois. It recognizes the social and historical backdrop that shaped these “classical” sociological ideas and concepts, notably influenced by imperialism and colonialism. This historical context notably sidelined the voices of BIPOC (Black, Indigenous, and People of Color) and women. Consequently, fundamental concepts like race and gender received inadequate theoretical attention within “classical” sociology. To bridge this gap, the course will prioritize students ’ interests and intellectual needs.
courses.legacyDescription: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
courses.contribution: introduces social theory and institutions in socio-historical and global context

courses.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
courses.profile: Similar to their quantitative counterparts, qualitative researchers ask basic, but demanding, questions before they start making any enquires, e.g. What is truth? What is reality? What is knowledge? Why do we want to conduct research? What do we want to get out of it? In contrast to quantitative studies, however, qualitative researchers are less interested in numbers, trends and generalisations. Instead, they are keen to explore the messiness of social processes: what motivates people to take actions, how people make sense of their world, and how politics, history and cultures influence people’s thinking and actions. In this course, we will critically examine the four key stages of conducting qualitative research: (1) research design and preparation; (2) data collection and management; (3) data analysis and interpretation, and (4) research dissemination. Throughout the course, students are expected to take an active role – to form a research group and choose a research topic, to interrogate qualitative research theories and their own research experiences, and to critically reflect the research processes and students’ own positionality, biases and assumptions. At the end of the course, students will share their research findings and experiences with one another.
courses.legacyDescription: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
courses.contribution: teaches qualitative design, interpretation, reflexivity, data collection and dissemination

courses.name: Modern Sociology
courses.profile: Examines the trajectory of sociology within the culture of imperialism and colonial responses. Studies leading social theories and debates about modernity and critically engages with sociological discourses.
courses.legacyDescription: Examines the trajectory of sociology within the culture of imperialism and colonial responses. Studies leading social theories and debates about modernity and critically engages with sociological discourses.
courses.contribution: examines modernity, imperialism, colonial responses and the development of social theory

courses.name: Social Movements & Environmental Justice
courses.profile: Focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice. Uses case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas and integrates perspectives such as feminism, anti‑colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding to encourage civic engagement.
courses.legacyDescription: Focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice. Uses case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas and integrates perspectives such as feminism, anti‑colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding to encourage civic engagement.
courses.contribution: studies social movements, anti-colonialism, feminism and environmental justice through cases

courses.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
courses.profile: The course ‘GOSSOCI311 New Issues in Contemporary Sociology’ builds upon the topics covered in ‘GOSSOCI101 Introduction to Sociology’ and ‘GOSSOCI202 Modern Sociology’. Its primary goal is to familiarise students with significant debates in sociological theory from a global perspective. This edition of the course focuses specifically on the idea of civil society, examining topics such as solidarity, social capital, social trust, the public and civil sphere, and civil repair in modern societies. The first part of the course explores a critical approach to civil society, starting with Gramsci’s ideas, followed by Habermas’s ideas on the public sphere and Fraser’s critique. It will examine cases in the Global South, and we will watch and discuss a movie about the power of grassroots civil society. The second part focuses on Alexander’s work on the Civil Sphere, cases of civil repair in Latin America, and performances of solidarity with migrants along Europe's southern border. The final part will explore the decolonial critique of the classical approaches to civil society and the civil sphere. Alongside the theoretical component, the course also includes an empirical aspect. Students will select an NGO, voluntary organisation, or other Civil Society Organisation (CSO) to explore the concepts covered in the course and the challenges associated with the work undertaken by these organisations. Using a Community Engaged Learning (CEL) approach, students will observe and study an organisation throughout the semester to gain an understanding of its culture, impact, and challenges.
courses.legacyDescription: Examines contemporary sociological debates about civil society through critical tradition, neo‑functionalism and decolonial critiques. Includes research group projects with NGOs or civil society organizations that translate conceptual insights into empirical analysis.
courses.contribution: develops advanced global social theory around civil society, solidarity, trust and institutional repair

courses.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
courses.profile: Tweets by politicians and celebrities. Social media conspiracy theories. Product advertising. Anti-war protests. Speeches about justice. These are all examples of rhetorical discourse. Both the internet and history books are full of examples of the relevance of the art of rhetoric, as are our daily lives. Plato defined rhetoric as the “art of enchanting the soul”, while Aristotle considered it the ability to “discover in any particular case, all of the available means of persuasion". Quintilian, on the other hand, simply considered rhetoric to be “the art of the good person speaking well”. Whatever the definition, mastering this art often involves more work than is often imagined; work that is at the core of this course. This course is a fundamentally a skills course, even if there is a significant amount of rhetorical history and theory. No effective standpoint can be formed, no supporting arguments found, no paper written, no presentation given, no textual analysis conducted without knowledge of how rhetoric works. Therefore, it is necessary for students to have a proper understanding of what rhetoric is and what it involves, and also how rhetoric can be applied consciously. This course offers the skills that students will need to be able to structure any future academic essay or future oral presentation in a clear, persuasive and academic way. The course starts by considering the Greek and Roman Western roots of rhetoric. It focuses on the canons of rhetoric applied to the three main types of argumentation, i.e.
courses.legacyDescription: Teaches how to craft persuasive messages, influence opinions, inspire action and connect people. Draws on historical communicators from Aristotle to Barack Obama and applies stylistic techniques to students’ own writing and speaking.
courses.contribution: Specific complementary rhetorical analysis, academic essay structure and oral argument support communication of historical inquiry; this is not historical source criticism.

courses.name: Rhetoric in Action
courses.profile: To what extent can students on an undergraduate rhetoric course at a liberal art and science college empower a group of local primary school children to become more confident and more persuasive public speakers and debaters? This is the question that this course sets out to explore in this practice-based ‘Rhetoric in Action’ module. In this course, students will learn about the theory and practice of the public work of rhetoric. They will also learn about what Community Engaged Learning is and about how it will shape their roles during this course. After an introduction to these theories, the students will then be trained in several public speaking, debating and storytelling exercises that will build on what they have already learned in the 100-level rhetoric class. With their new didactic skills and knowledge, they will then design several innovative public speaking and debating exercises for the school children. Before the mid-term break, the teaching and learning space will shift from the UCR classroom to local school Magistraal. The students will then work with small groups of primary school children and their teachers. These children are sometimes from socio-economically disadvantaged groups and are aged between 9 and 12. The language of interaction will principally be Dutch, but English, and even Arabic, may come into play in certain cases. The UCR students will be teaching and training the school children in the different forms of public address that they have themselves designed.
courses.legacyDescription: Develops persuasive speaking skills by applying rhetorical theory in the real world. Students work with local primary school children, building public-speaking skills and empowering them to find their voices.
courses.contribution: Specific complementary public rhetoric and community-engaged teaching with primary-school pupils develop practical communication; no specialist public-history placement is claimed.

courses.name: Introduction to Western Art History
courses.profile: This course provides a chronological overview of Western art history from the early Renaissance to the present. It emphasizes key paintings that define specific periods or movements, exploring the works and their creators in detail. The course also considers the impact of art institutions, markets, critics, and historiographers on the legacy of these masterpieces. Focusing on major stylistic movements in Europe and the Americas, the course lays the groundwork for advanced art history studies. It introduces essential tools for visual analysis and interpretation, fostering an understanding of how visual culture reflects historical contexts and societal values.
courses.legacyDescription: Provides an introduction to Western art history, tracing major artistic movements from the late Middle Ages to the present. Through close study of key paintings and their makers, students gain insight into evolving styles, techniques and cultural influences.
courses.contribution: surveys Western art from the Renaissance to the present and teaches visual and historiographical analysis

courses.name: Introduction to World Archaeology
courses.profile: How does making things define human existence and societies, from their earliest beginnings to the end of antiquity and beyond? This course examines this question first, through the pragmatics of manufacture in relation to religious, social, and gendered identities, from Çatalhöyük (Türkiye) in 10.000 BCE and the region of Kush (Sudan) around 8.000 BCE, to classical Athens and Rome, and from the Harappan Valley to the Philippines. In every context we will explore the artefacts, their production and their makers. By exploring these, we can discover the story of the communities that made them. We will look at individual manufacturing techniques from settlements in different parts of the world, and how the objects made in (urban) communities could help people negotiate identity. We will look at the social and environmental impact of these crafts, and how technologies have helped shape social identity through the ancient world. The course has an experimental component where we design an educational activity surrounding an archaeological or ancient craft-related theme, for which a main requirement is that it involves a hands-on activity. Finally, we will explore how archaeological research methods can be used in contemporary settings.
courses.legacyDescription: Explores ancient craft production from around the world. Examines how making objects shaped human development and how ancient solutions can inform modern sustainability.
courses.contribution: Direct ancient material-culture and archaeological methods examine making, social identities and environmental effects; its chronology complements the mainly modern historical core.

courses.name: African Art & Heritage
courses.profile: This course offers an introduction to African art and heritage, with a special focus on the rich artistic traditions of western Africa. Students will study the region’s diverse visual languages, uncovering how sculptures, masks, and other forms of visual expression embody cultural, religious, and social meaning. The course also traces Africa’s enduring influence on global art, from the appropriations of European artists like Picasso and Matisse to modern and contemporary African and African diaspora artists who reinterpret traditional forms in often unexpected ways. A significant component of the course addresses ethical and institutional questions surrounding the collection and display of African art. Through case studies and critical debate, students will explore the legacy of colonial-era looting, the politics of museum acquisitions, and the growing movement for repatriation of African art to their place of origin. Designed for students interested in art history, cultural heritage, and museum studies, the course encourages you to see African art not just as objects, but as living stories: resilient, resonant, and still unfolding.
courses.legacyDescription: Examines the artistic, historical and ethical dimensions of African art. Highlights distinct forms and cultural significance, considers influence on Western modernism and addresses looting, colonial-era acquisitions and repatriation efforts.
courses.contribution: studies African art, heritage, colonial appropriation, cultural meaning and repatriation

courses.name: Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean
courses.legacyDescription: This course examines the painting, sculpture, and architecture of Renaissance Italy and the extensive artistic connections that linked the Italian peninsula to other regions of the world. By exploring a range of geographical contexts, from the Islamic courts of the Eastern Mediterranean and the commercial routes connecting Europe, Asia, and Africa to the newly encountered territories of the Americas, students will examine how trade, colonization, and cross-cultural exchange shaped the production and meaning of Renaissance art.
courses.contribution: places Renaissance Italy in the connected cultural history of the global Mediterranean

courses.name: Modern Art & Modern Museums
courses.profile: This course examines key debates on modern art through a carefully selected range of themes and topics. A central focus is the relationship between art and its presentation in museums and exhibitions. By exploring curatorial practices and exhibition strategies, students will gain insight into how art institutions shape public perception and understanding of modern and contemporary art.
courses.legacyDescription: Examines debates on modern art through various themes. Focuses on the relationship between art and its presentation in museums and exhibitions, exploring curatorial practices and exhibition strategies.
courses.contribution: Direct cultural-history contribution through modern art, museums, exhibitions and curatorial practices shaping public understanding; not general public-history professional training.

courses.name: Writing Art's Histories
courses.legacyDescription: This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.
courses.contribution: Direct art-historical historiography: critical readings examine the history, ideas and methodologies of art history, interpretation and authorship. A separate required research-writing project is not established.

courses.name: Introduction to Literary Studies
courses.profile: Literature is common ground. It is ground not managed wholly by commercial interests, nor can it be strip-mined like popular culture…There’s a lot of talk about the tame world versus the wild world. It is not only a wild nature that we need as human beings; it is the untamed open space of our imaginations. Reading is where the wild things are. Jeannette Winterson Why Be Happy When You Can Be Normal. London, Vintage, 2012, p.144 The course is an introduction into practical criticism and literary interpretation. It explores some basic issues of literary study starting from the questions: what is literature, why do we read it, and why do we study it? The course familiarises students with formal properties of a literary work, makes them aware of a constructed character of literary text, and opens discussion of literary value. It is based on a classic division into three major genres (fiction, poetry and drama), supplemented by contemporary non-fiction, and rudiments of film narration. The goal of the course is to provide students with basic critical terms, tools and techniques that will make them sensitive readers and enhance their appreciation of a literary work.
courses.legacyDescription: Introduces what literature is, why we read it and how to interpret it. Covers fiction, poetry, drama, non‑fiction and film narration, exploring various literary forms and genres such as graphic narratives and romance novels.
courses.contribution: provides methods for interpreting literary and narrative forms as cultural evidence

courses.name: Film & Text
courses.profile: It is a researched fact that more than 50% of films have their literary originals. More than three-quarters of the American Academy Awards have been granted to films based on novels, short stories and dramas. There are plentiful examples of famous films based on no less famous literary texts, from the already hackneyed Pride and Prejudice, through Bridget Jones’ Diary, The Lord of the Rings, the Narnia cycle, A Passage to India, Batman, A Thousand and One Nights to Frankenstein, Dracula, Ninety Eighty-Four and Hamlet. This close relation between literature and film becomes even clearer when we realize that film is a text that tells a story. Keeping this in mind, in this course we will discuss various ways in which a literary original is translated on screen, tracing various links between literary and film narration, and various intertextual dimensions of film adaptation. The course offers instruction in a methodology of film analysis, building on students’ knowledge of literature, media and popular culture. As it studies manifold transactions between the adaptor, the critic and the viewers, it is vital to every student interested in literature, media, popular culture and journalism. Our first step is the basic formalist analysis of a literary text along with its plot, structure, character, setting, and a formalist analysis of the multi-track film (image, acting, music, sound effects) along with its “syntax” and “diction” which all contribute to its tone and themes.
courses.legacyDescription: Studies complex links between literary and film narratives. Analyzes formal aspects of both media, discusses adaptation, intertextuality, viewer participation and narrative dynamics, and allows students to research topics like literature‑to‑film adaptation and cross‑cultural themes.
courses.contribution: compares literary texts and film through cultural analysis and interpretive strategies

courses.name: Media & Race
courses.profile: Whose stories are remembered and whose are erased? What do the stories un/told teach us about power, privilege, and resistance? How do cultural expressions and forms like film, photographs, and music address systemic racism, critique the present, and envision just futures? These questions steer this course. Addressing them reveals links between past and present that students explore in final podcasts grounded in research and fueled by passion. Race, at the heart of American history and life, is at the center of this class. We begin in the late 19th century with the “end” of slavery and continue into the 21st century with the advent of ICE. Throughout the term we explore the ways media supports systems of oppression and empowers the oppressed.
courses.legacyDescription: Investigates storytelling and power in relation to race. Examines Afrofuturism and systemic racism and guides students in creating podcasts that explore links between past and present.
courses.contribution: connects past and present through stories of race, power, erasure, resistance and public memory

courses.name: The Documentary
courses.profile: In this course we will discuss the development of the documentary form and discover various techniques used by documentary film makers. We start by tracing the documentary film from its origins (e.g. including the work of pioneer documentarians like Dziga Vertov and Robert Flaherty) to the present. We will analyze a large number of non-fiction representations of the world and its people, focusing on a range of documentary styles and genres and rooting this diversity in its various historical and social contexts, as well as considering the ethical and aesthetic aspects of documentaries. The course primarily considers documentary film, but we will also explore the genre through other media forms, including audio productions, allowing students to develop skills useful in an increasingly multimodal culture. Assessment includes a presentation, the production of a very short documentary item, an essay-type exam and several small homework assignments on Moodle. Input to help shape this course is highly appreciated.
courses.legacyDescription: Introduces development of the documentary form. Students write a theoretical paper and produce a short documentary film, fostering understanding of documentary diversity and providing analytical tools for documentary study.
courses.contribution: traces documentary history and develops critical and practical analysis of non-fiction representation

finalDecisions.rationale: Both survey modern political, economic and cultural change across a broad chronological and international frame; UCR begins in 1815 rather than 1500.
Both compare societies through global encounters and unequal power; UCR ranges across empires more broadly and is not confined to 1300-1800.
The external modern-societies survey is not reproduced by a separate UCR course; UCR’s broad Modern History course is already shown with Global History.
Both analyse colonialism, identity, belonging and changing historical orders; UCR concentrates on Native American histories.

Partial research relationship: UCR investigates primary sources on the 1809 Walcheren Expedition and writes a substantial paper. The external class prepares a separate thesis in the chosen Economic History focus area.

The UCR History Research Seminar develops historical research at advanced level but is already aligned to the comparator's focus-area thesis class; UCR has no separate introductory Becoming a Historian course.
UCR courses repeatedly connect past and present, but there is no separate historiography-and-contemporary-relevance course matching Rethinking History.
UCR offers philosophy courses, but none of the scheduled courses is a dedicated philosophy-of-history course.
The comparator requires a 15-EC individual History thesis. None of the 24 scheduled UCR courses is a thesis, so UCR's optional independent-research element is displayed alongside it.
The comparator component is an open History elective, while UCR elective choice is distributed throughout each 180-EC pathway; no single scheduled course is asserted as its equivalent.
Both teach research design and statistical analysis; the comparator applies those methods specifically to historical data.
Both teach systematic qualitative collection and interpretation; the comparator specialises in historical sources and techniques such as discourse, narrative and oral-history analysis.

Partial skill relationship in academic argument, essay structure and speaking. UCR teaches general rhetoric; the external component is specifically historical writing. No unchanged word-count requirement is assumed from older overview copy.
UCR has public rhetoric and civic formation, but no scheduled course specifically trains the public role of historians.
The comparator's 15-EC minor is an open external-field choice. UCR breadth is distributed across the full liberal-arts curriculum, so no one scheduled course is treated as the minor.
The selected comparator route requires a 15-EC field-specific internship. None of the scheduled UCR courses is an internship or equivalent workplace placement.

Partial relationship in international economic processes and trade. UCR teaches macroeconomic theory and policy; the external course studies economic globalisation and international power historically.
No selected UCR course establishes historical multinational–state relations.
The dedicated historical inquiry into emerging economies and global labour has no adequate selected-course correspondence.
Partial relationship in inequality, institutions and redistribution. UCR uses contemporary economic theory and evidence; the external component investigates capitalism and inequality historically.
Both introduce sociological concepts and theories as tools for understanding societies; the comparator applies them explicitly in historical research.
